title: Nolan's Odyssey is Forgettable
author: The Classical Dispatch
summary: Reviewing the reaction to Christopher Nolan's film adaptation of The Odyssey, the author argues that its central failure is not infidelity to Homer's plot but a failure to inhabit Homer's pagan worldview honestly enough to move an audience. Leaning on storyteller Martin Shaw's critique that the film was 'robbed of its essential pagan-ness,' the piece distinguishes between two concerns: whether an adaptation is faithful to the text, and whether it succeeds as a human story regardless of fidelity. It then engages critic Peter Leithart's counterargument that the Western canon has always freely rewritten Homer (citing Virgil, Shakespeare, and others), conceding the historical point but arguing Nolan's changes fail for a different reason — they don't honor the source deeply enough to be remembered, unlike Shakespeare's or Dante's revisions. The essay closes by invoking C.S. Lewis's argument that modern culture may need to pass back through genuine paganism en route to Christianity, framing Nolan's sanitized, secularized Odysseus as a missed opportunity to let the story do that work.
points: Distinguishes 'unfaithful to Homer' from 'fails as a story' — the first is a long Western tradition, the second is Nolan's actual failure.
A myth's power may depend on its 'pagan-ness' being taken seriously rather than softened for modern sensibility.
The Western canon's history of freely rewriting Homer (Virgil, Dante, Shakespeare) is not itself a defense — some rewrites honor the source enough to be remembered, others don't.
Invokes C.S. Lewis's claim that a post-Christian culture may need to become genuinely pagan again before it can become Christian, applying it to how myth should be adapted.
Judges an adaptation's legitimacy partly by whether its changes are 'good enough to remember,' not merely by fidelity to the original.
quotes: I'd love Odysseus to have a conversion experience on the beach, but it's not in the story. And what is in the story is humor, sex, wonderful language, and a world ensouled with gods and goddesses and a great kind of tragic beautiful story about nostos—about getting home.

The bad script notwithstanding, Shaw exposed what I think is its most fatal flaw: "I didn't care. I just didn't care about anybody. I didn't weep. And for me, as somebody that loves that story dearly." He summed it up as, "Visually sumptuous, emotionally vacuous.

Leithart points out some typical examples: Virgil, Dante, Tennyson, Auden, and others take liberties with the Homeric elements—the structure of the story, the heroic nature of Odysseus himself, the integrity of certain characters.

Long before Christopher Nolan, "woke" Will Shakespeare deconstructed one of Western civilization's founding stories. But that's what "the classics" do: plunder, rewrite, subvert, and twist earlier classics.

Modern attempts of retelling the old stories seem doomed to always get it wrong. If there is a tradition in Western art and literature of plundering and rewriting Homer, then Nolan seems outside of it.

In his essay "A Christmas Sermon for Pagans," C. S. Lewis writes, "It looks to me, neighbours, as though we shall have to set about becoming true Pagans if only as a preliminary to becoming Christians.
The changes of Nolan, however, are typical of modern retellings. They alter without being good enough to remember.
